I will keep it simple and do what fits my place, my age, and the way farming works in Quzhou County. I will plant the usual wheat-maize rotation on all my land. That is what I trust most because it matches the local climate, the irrigation conditions on the North China Plain, and the way I can spread labor through the year. I do not want to gamble on crops that need more market judgment or more delicate management. Winter wheat gives me a steady grain crop through spring, and then I can follow it directly with summer maize after harvest, so the land works for me all year. Since I have no formal schooling, I would rather use a familiar, standard system that I know how to manage well than chase something complicated.

For winter wheat, I will use an improved variety, not old saved seed. I want stable emergence, better disease resistance, and a safer yield. I will prepare the field with rotary tillage, put on base fertilizer, sow at the normal local time in autumn, and then focus on the key steps: one strong seedling stage, one jointing stage, one grain-filling stage. I will irrigate about three times if water is available: once after sowing or before winter if the soil is dry, once around jointing, and once around filling. I will keep fertilizer moderate because too much nitrogen makes wheat lodge and wastes money. I will spray only when needed, mainly for weeds early and then for disease or aphids later if pressure shows up. For summer maize, I will follow wheat immediately so I do not lose moisture or time. I will use hybrid seed because maize responds well to it and the yield is more dependable. I will mostly keep no-tillage after wheat harvest and direct seed into the stubble to save labor and hold soil moisture. I will give maize enough nitrogen, but not in a wasteful way, with part at planting and part later. I will irrigate only a couple of times if rainfall is short, mainly around the big demand period. My goal is not the highest possible yield on paper. My goal is a steady harvest, manageable work, and lower risk.
